Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette:
Ravi, a 44-year-old South Asian chef, still cannot put words to what he witnessed during the night his village was attacked. He remembers fragments—muzzle flashes, the wet sound of bodies hitting the ground, the smell of diesel and blood—but when he tries to tell anyone, the story dissolves into static. Sometimes, recalling it, he feels nothing, as if watching a stranger’s life; other times, a wave of grief hits him so hard he has to brace himself against the counter. That grief feeds a stubborn belief: he should have done more. He was hiding in a drainage ditch while his neighbors were dragged out. “I will never forgive myself,” he says flatly, certain he has permanently changed for the worse. That conviction—that he was a coward who had failed—meant he now saw threat in things he would once have dismissed: a stranger’s quick step, a slammed door, the bark of a dog in the alley.

Those beliefs make certain moments unbearable. An ambulance siren on his commute pins him in place, sweat breaking out. A coworker recounting a fender bender makes his vision narrow. When a guest walks into the restaurant with a bandaged hand, Ravi’s throat closes—he has to retreat to the walk-in cooler. Each trigger cranks his vigilance higher. He scans the dining room for exits before he can take an order, checks the kitchen door obsessively, and finds himself unable to follow a simple recipe because his mind is tripping over escape routes. Living at that pitch of alertness, he found that ordinary cues—a dropped plate, a raised hand, a car horn outside—now hit him as emergency signals, each one pulling his attention away from the task at hand.

To manage, Ravi has developed habits that feel protective but steadily shrink his world. He detours three blocks to avoid a police substation. But the detour itself had become a trigger: every time he took that longer route he relived the reason for the avoidance, and the streets he walked became saturated with the memory of what he was running from. He refuses shifts at the patio grill—an open space where he feels exposed. By never staying in an open space long enough to discover it was safe, his nervous system received no evidence to update its assessment—the threat remained as high as the night of the attack, uncalibrated and unbroken. And when the head chef raises his voice over a burned sauce, Ravi’s response is not anger but a sickening compliance; he apologizes excessively, offers to scrub floors, does whatever will make the threat dissolve. This fawning leaves him hollow, and afterward he replays the memory of the attack with fresh self-disgust: See, you’re still a coward. The guilt magnifies his sensitivity, so the next ambulance seems even louder, the next wound even more vivid.

The hypervigilance itself keeps the trauma raw. On high-alert days, Ravi cannot summon a coherent narrative of the event—only images and sensations that seem to belong to someone else. That emotional distance then deepens his guilt: “If I was really a survivor, wouldn’t I feel something real?” He has stopped seeing his remaining family because gatherings involve talk of accidents or travel dangers, and anyway, he cannot focus on their stories. At work, his concentration slips; he misreads tickets, double‑salt a sauce, and the head chef’s irritation only makes Ravi more watchful, more compliant.

The cycle tightens. Each avoided space reinforces the belief that he is irretrievably broken, which in turn makes the next uniform or siren feel catastrophic. He now plans his entire week around possible trigger encounters—checking the neighborhood for police cars before he leaves the house, scanning lunch menus for any dish that might remind him of the camp. The exhaustion is constant. What finally brought Ravi to a clinic was a night shift when a delivery driver walked in with a gash on his arm. Ravi froze, then fawned so hard he offered to do the driver’s paperwork; afterward he vomited in the alley. He is afraid he will lose his job, but more than that, he is afraid that the permanent damage he already feels is the only truth. That verdict — that he is irreparably broken and a coward — had led him to decline every invitation from his remaining relatives, because he believed they would see the truth of his failure and confirm his own worst judgment.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals cause the occurrence or increased detection of triggers; instead, appraisals only amplify the emotional impact of existing triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not show that a heightened sense of threat leads to more frequent or intense triggering stimuli; threat affects memory and strategies but not triggers directly.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette describes maladaptive strategies as responses to triggers, not as causes of new trigger experiences.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: Maladaptive strategies are shown to affect negative appraisals and memory, but there is no direct causal link from strategies to an increased sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
